newsitem.title: USA: Wall St stocks finish higher, extending record run.
newsitem.headline: Wall St stocks finish higher, extending record run.

text.p: U.S. stocks closed moderately higher on Monday, extending their trek into record territory.

The Dow industrials gained 43 points to end unofficially at 7479, the second straight record finish for blue chips. Including the day's gains, the Dow has surged more than 1,000 points since the start of 1997.

Though the session lacked the sheer firepower displayed last Friday -- when the Dow leapt 130.49 points -- it brought the S&P's 500 index and the New York Stock Exchange, American Stock Exchange and Nasdaq composites to all-time highs.
Leading the rally among blue chips were technology and drug stocks, as investors focused on the potential export benefits of a weaker U.S. dollar.

Over the last five weeks, the dollar has fallen sharply against the Japanese yen and has recently begun struggling against the German mark, which has firmed on mounting uncertainty over issues related to European Monetary Union.

"For the most part, the groups going up today you could cover with the umbrella of exports," said Greg Nie, technical analyst at EVEREN Securities. "Techs and drug companies are both beneficiaries of a declining dollar."

Among Dow stocks, International Business Machines Corp rose 1-1/4 to 86-7/8 and Hewlett-Packard Co gained 1-1/8 to 53-3/8. Johnson & Johnson added 1-1/2 to 61-5/8 and Merck and Co Inc rose 1-1/2 to 93-3/4.
Shares in cable television companies jumped amid a flurry of high-profile industry deals.

Comcast Corp jumped 2-13/16 to 21-1/16 after Microsoft Corp agreed to make a $1 billion investment in the company, a move that significantly broadens the leading software company's reach in the television business.

Cablevision Systems Corp surged 9-1/2 to 44-1/8 after it said it would buy 10 cable systems in the New York area from Tele-Communications Inc for stock worth more than $500 million, after factoring in the day's gains.
The developments sparked life into the cable sector, which had languished for some time, with the Microsoft deal in particular serving as a wake-up call, analysts said.

"I think the deal forced everyone to step back and remember that cable is going to be a big player in the future of telecommunications," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds.

Finaincial stocks ended lower. The group was an indirect casualty of the declining dollar, which contributed to a weak performance in the bond market. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell 18/32, pushing the yield up to 6.82 percent.
One bank that bucked the trend was BankAmerica Corp, which rose 3/4 to 124.

The company announced two major deals -- to acquire privately held San Francisco-based investment bank Robertson Stephens & Co for about $540 million, and to sell its Security Pacific Financial Services unit to Travelers Group Inc for $1.6 billion.

The BankAmerica-Robertson Stephens pact fueled interest in brokerage shares, where consolidation expectations have been an ongoing theme. Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette jumped 4-5/8 to 56-3/8 and Legg Mason Inc added 2-7/8 to 49-1/8.
The S&P 500 rose 4.90 points to 862.91, the NYSE Composite rose 2.04 points to 450.17, the Nasdaq Composite rose 7.20 points to 1412.04 and the Amex Composite rose 4.92 points to 619.57, all records.
